questions.stem: A client develops focal bone pain, warmth, swelling, and fever several weeks after a deep puncture wound to the foot. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Cellulitis limited to superficial soft tissue without involvement of underlying bone","B":"Osteomyelitis caused by infection involving bone after the penetrating foot injury","C":"Deep vein thrombosis caused primarily by venous stasis from prolonged immobility","D":"Acute gout caused by urate crystal deposition in the first metatarsophalangeal joint"}}
questions.rationale: Penetrating trauma can directly inoculate organisms and lead to osteomyelitis. Focal bone pain with local warmth or swelling and systemic symptoms such as fever warrants evaluation for bone infection.
questions.source_detail: History and Physical; contiguous/direct-inoculation osteomyelitis after trauma; last update May 31, 2023; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A severely malnourished client begins nutritional support. Which laboratory pattern is most concerning for refeeding syndrome?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Stable phosphate with isolated mild sodium elevation after feeding has been restarted","B":"Rising phosphate with concurrent increases in potassium and magnesium after feeding starts","C":"Falling phosphate with concurrent decreases in potassium and magnesium after feeding starts","D":"Stable potassium and magnesium with isolated mild calcium elevation after feeding starts"}}
questions.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is characterized by clinically important electrolyte shifts after calories are reintroduced, particularly hypophosphatemia and often hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. These abnormalities can cause serious cardiac and neurologic complications.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — Consensus Recommendations for Refeeding Syndrome
questions.source_detail: ASPEN consensus recommendations, Nutrition in Clinical Practice 2020; diagnostic/electrolyte framework for refeeding syndrome; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: An older adult has poor oral intake and possible dehydration. How should the nurse interpret skin turgor during the assessment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Skin turgor is unrelated to hydration assessment and should never be examined clinically","B":"Skin turgor is more reliable in older adults because aging increases dermal elasticity","C":"Skin turgor alone is sufficient to rule out dehydration when recoil appears normal","D":"Skin turgor is less reliable in older adults because normal aging reduces skin elasticity"}}
questions.rationale: Age-related loss of skin elasticity makes skin turgor less reliable for assessing dehydration in older adults. Hydration assessment should incorporate additional findings rather than relying on turgor alone.
questions.source_name: Deißler et al. — Hydration Status Assessment in Older Patients (2023)
questions.source_detail: Review of hydration assessment in adults ≥65 years: reduced skin turgor and multiple other classic clinical signs lack sufficient diagnostic accuracy; skin turgor correlates with age more than hydration status.

questions.stem: A client has a serum sodium of 152 mEq/L with intense thirst, restlessness, and confusion. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hypernatremia, commonly reflecting a relative free-water deficit and causing neurologic symptoms","B":"Hyponatremia, commonly reflecting excess free water and producing the measured sodium value","C":"Hyperkalemia, because potassium excess directly explains an elevated measured sodium level","D":"A normal sodium concentration, because symptoms are unrelated to the laboratory measurement"}}
questions.rationale: A sodium concentration above the usual reference range is hypernatremia. It commonly reflects water deficit relative to sodium and may produce thirst and neurologic manifestations such as restlessness or confusion.
questions.source_detail: High blood sodium (hypernatremia) and associated symptoms/causes; U.S. National Library of Medicine; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client's red blood cell count is clearly below the laboratory reference interval. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The finding is most consistent with polycythemia and excessive circulating red cell mass","B":"The finding can support evaluation for anemia and reduced oxygen-carrying red cell mass","C":"The finding confirms normal hematologic status without need for clinical correlation","D":"The finding specifically diagnoses iron deficiency without considering any other causes"}}
questions.rationale: A low RBC count can occur with anemia, but RBC count alone does not determine the cause. The result should be interpreted with hemoglobin, hematocrit, indices, symptoms, and clinical context.

questions.stem: A client with chest pain has an elevated CK-MB value. Which statement best reflects current cardiac biomarker practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"CK-MB primarily evaluates renal filtration and has no recognized relationship to myocardium","B":"CK-MB is more cardiac-specific than troponin and should replace serial troponin testing","C":"CK-MB can indicate myocardial injury, but cardiac troponin is the preferred biomarker today","D":"CK-MB alone proves acute myocardial infarction regardless of symptoms, ECG, or serial testing"}}
questions.rationale: CK-MB may rise with myocardial injury, but current chest-pain guidance identifies cardiac troponin, especially high-sensitivity troponin, as the preferred biomarker for myocardial injury. Biomarkers require clinical and ECG correlation.
questions.source_name: ACC/AHA — 2021 Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain
questions.source_detail: Biomarkers section: serial cardiac troponin I/T is preferred for myocardial injury; high-sensitivity troponin preferred; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client asks what a stool-based occult blood screening test does. Which explanation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It looks for blood not visible to the eye; a positive screening result needs follow-up evaluation","B":"It directly visualizes the entire colon and can remove suspicious polyps during the same test","C":"It confirms colorectal cancer by itself, so a positive result eliminates need for colonoscopy","D":"It measures serum tumor markers and is unrelated to blood that may be present in the stool"}}
questions.rationale: Stool blood tests detect occult blood and are screening tests, not definitive cancer diagnoses. A positive stool-based screening test requires follow-up colonoscopy to determine the source.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks how coagulation factors contribute to hemostasis after blood-vessel injury. Which response is correct?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"They act only after a clot is fully formed and function mainly to dissolve the existing fibrin mesh","B":"They activate in a sequence that generates fibrin and helps stabilize the developing platelet plug","C":"They are identical to platelets and therefore have no separate role in secondary hemostasis","D":"They prevent platelet adhesion and keep fibrin from forming at the site of vascular injury"}}
questions.rationale: Coagulation factors activate through coordinated pathways that culminate in thrombin generation and fibrin formation. Fibrin stabilizes the platelet plug and supports formation of a durable clot.
questions.source_detail: Blood clotting process: clotting factors and fibrin stabilize the platelet plug; National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute; accessed 2026-08-14.
